summary:
West Papua operates no provincial criminal law reaching sexual conduct or gender expression. The province stands under Indonesia's national framework without local additions, and no regency-level regulation on dress, public morality or gender presentation is documented in this inventory.

Security-force conduct is the province's defining documented risk. A report published on 22 July 2025 by the Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network recorded 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment by police and military against people in detention in Maybrat and the Central Highlands through early 2025, with most victims male and under 24, seven female, and seven minors aged 15 to 17; the report's framing is 'impunity, secrecy and silence', indicating near-total absence of accountability. Any visitor to the province, including a visibly gender-nonconforming one, stands in this security-force environment.

The Papua human-rights monitor's Q3 2025 quarterly records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025. In Sorong, police arrested over a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans. No trans-specific finding accompanies this pattern, but it amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor.

Provincial document practice follows the national pattern: since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with Kartu Tanda Penduduk, including residents of Papua, but the card recognises only 'male' and 'female' with no third gender or X designator, and prints gender at birth unless a court recognition is obtained. Families' disapproval can block the documentation process, which officials cite as leaving some residents undocumented and unable to access work or social services.

Legal gender recognition is available nationally after sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, after which the person may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. The judicial system has recognised trans status: Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar was the first trans Indonesian legally recognised as female, and there are documented cases where perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community were arrested and prosecuted.

Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment. The Indonesian Ulama Council ruled that transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating that if they are 'not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously' they must be willing 'to accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed'. This religious-body position sits alongside the judicial system's contrary practice.

Targeted enforcement documented against trans people includes the January 2018 North Aceh police arrest of twelve transgender women, during which their hair was forcibly cut, they were compelled into men's clothing, and beauty salons were closed. The Jakarta Social Agency declared waria socially dysfunctional and conducted regular raids and incarceration in city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres alongside homeless people, beggars and buskers, requiring documentation and a signed pledge before release; officials stated this was intended as a deterrent against being transgender and warned that continued violations would result in jail time. These are national-level actions, not West Papua ones, but they set the enforcement backdrop.

Discrimination in employment is documented: transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are frequently pushed into prostitution and other informal or illegal activity to survive, with discrimination and harassment described as not uncommon though violence as quite rare. The article also notes that gays in jails are often sexually abused because of their orientation and do not report it, due to trauma and fear of return.

The control environment includes the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction, which prohibits presentations suggesting same-sex relations and carries a fine or up to seven years' imprisonment; a March 2016 broadcasting commission policy banning programmes that make LGBTQ behaviour appear 'normal' and discouraging effeminate, transgender or cross-dressing figures; bans on sites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ terms including Grindr; and widely practiced, openly advertised conversion therapy, including rehabilitation-centre treatment with de facto legalisation by some city governments after the 'RUU Ketahanan Keluarga' Family Resilience draft was rejected by 5 of 9 factions.

Care context: a 2012 Health Ministry estimate put the number of transgender women at around 31 thousand. Yayasan Srikandi Sejati, founded 1998, focuses on transgender health, providing HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic, operating amid a lack of school sex education and a historical movement focus that led the public to believe AIDS was a 'gay disease'.

Cultural context: transgender identity, also called waria, has long been part of Indonesian culture and society, and some public tolerance is given to transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry. The article states that while transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have in recent years faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more popular in Indonesia.

Military service context: in 2021 Aprilio Manganang became the first service member to legally change gender from female to male, though his case involved an intersex person assigned female at birth and raised as a girl.
tangentialFactors:
The province's documented risk profile is dominated by general security-force violence rather than trans-specific harm. The Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network's 22 July 2025 report and the Papua human-rights monitor's Q3 2025 quarterly describe military and police conduct affecting the population broadly; no trans-specific incident is recorded in this inventory for West Papua.

Comparatively, the national picture carries documented trans-specific enforcement (the January 2018 North Aceh arrests, Jakarta Social Agency raids) that West Papua itself does not reproduce in this inventory. A visitor's exposure in West Papua is therefore shaped more by the general security environment and by national-level document and recognition rules than by provincial trans-targeted policing.

Racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans, recorded alongside displacement in the Q3 2025 quarterly, is a further axis of exposure for a visitor who is both gender-nonconforming and read as an outsider.
localsOnly:
Transgender West Papuan residents can access the national legal gender recognition route: sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval permits a change of gender on official documents and thereafter marriage to someone of the opposite legal gender. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue Kartu Tanda Penduduk to transgender Indonesians including Papua residents, but the card carries only 'male' or 'female' and prints gender at birth absent court recognition.

Residents face the national control environment: the 2006 anti-pornography law, the March 2016 broadcasting commission policy, website and app bans, and openly advertised conversion therapy with de facto local-government legalisation in some cities. The Indonesian Ulama Council's position that transgender persons must live in their birth gender, and its statement that those unwilling to be 'cured' must accept ridicule and harassment, shapes the local social climate.

Employment discrimination pushes trans residents who do not conceal their identity out of legitimate work and into survival economies including sex work. Yayasan Srikandi Sejati, founded 1998, provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers through a free health clinic.

Protection machinery available to residents is limited: a 2015 police circular to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, National Police Regulation No. 8 of 2009 stipulating a duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation, and theoretical constitutional and Human Rights Law No. 39/1999 guarantees against employment discrimination on any ground. No specific law protects citizens from discrimination or harassment based on gender identity as of 2019.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network's 138 recorded acts of torture or ill-treatment include any trans or gender-nonconforming victims is not stated in this inventory; the victim breakdown given is by age and sex only.

No trans-specific incident, arrest, raid or recognition case is documented for West Papua itself in this inventory. All trans-specific enforcement examples (North Aceh 2018, Jakarta Social Agency) are from other provinces and are carried here only as national-framework context.

The Q3 2025 quarterly's displacement and racial-tension findings are not broken down by gender identity, so any trans-specific dimension to that pattern is unresolved.

Whether the national penal code provision in force since 2 January 2026 has been invoked in West Papua is not documented here.
